item.title: EU leaders seek to agree on a budget deal and a new loan for Ukraine
item.description:
EU leaders seek to agree on a budget deal and a new loan for Ukraine
European Union leaders are struggling to agree on a long-term budget and more money for Ukraine in the shape of a new $49 billion loanByLORNE COOK Associated PressNovember 25, 2026, 11:35 AM
Share
BRUSSELS -- European Union leaders struggled on Thursday to bridge major differences over the bloc’s long-term budget and agree a new $49 billion loan to help Ukraine meet its economic and military needs next year.
At a summit in Brussels, some leaders called for belts to be tightened, while others defended traditional policies that consume large parts of the budget. Most want extra funds for important new priorities, and to help Ukraine almost five years into the war.
“Europe needs solid finances. We can’t and we mustn’t take on more debt,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said, in remarks that highlighted some of the contradictions. “At the same time there is a series of tasks we must fulfill reliably.”
“The priorities must be a flourishing economy, the internal market must be able to develop its full potential, and we need better defense,” he told reporters.
The new joint spending package is a statement of the EU’s ambitions in the world. It’s small compared to national budgets and is financed mostly by the 27 member countries based on the size of their economies.
The 2028-2034 plan could amount to between 1% and 1.2% of gross national income, but it appears increasingly likely that the leaders might well miss an end-of-year goal to agree on it.
Germany is one of an important group of so-called net contributors that pay more into the budget than they get back in allocations, along with Austria, the Netherlands and Sweden, among others.
“The budget needs to be modernized and needs to be downsized if we want to strike a deal,” Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said as he arrived for the summit. “I’m ready for this marathon, if it ends today, tomorrow or somewhere in December.”

item.title: UK nuclear test veterans win 40-year battle for inquiry into Cold War tests
item.description:
UK nuclear test veterans win 40-year battle for inquiry into Cold War tests
Britain’s prime minister has authorized an inquiry into the impact of nuclear weapons tests on military veterans after a 40-year campaign by survivors who say they were used as guinea pigs for tests that damaged their health and that of their childrenByDANICA KIRKA Associated PressNovember 25, 2026, 7:06 AM
LONDON -- Britain’s prime minister has authorized an inquiry into the impact of nuclear weapons tests on military veterans after a 40-year campaign by survivors who say they were used as guinea pigs for tests that damaged their health and that of their children.
Andy Burnham made the announcement Tuesday night on the BBC’s “Newsnight” program, saying the panel’s chairman would be “relentless in his pursuit of the facts.” An estimated 22,000 British military personnel witnessed Cold War-era nuclear weapons tests in the Indian and Pacific oceans from 1952 to 1967.
“Nuclear test veterans and their families have waited too long for the truth, and that’s exactly what the independent panel will establish,” Burnham said in a statement.
Veterans claim Britain’s Ministry of Defense intentionally hid data from blood and urine samples that would demonstrate how they were unwittingly used as test subjects to investigate the impact of nuclear explosions on humans.
Former Defense Minister Tobias Ellwood said in September that he had “inadvertently misled” Parliament in 2018 when he told lawmakers the ministry had been unable to locate any information about such blood testing. He later learned that blood samples were taken throughout the military, although veterans seeking compensation for serious illnesses related to radiation exposure were unable to access them.
“This is among the greatest scandals in Britain, and it must be addressed,” Ellwood wrote in the Guardian.

item.title: Nigeria seizes $220 million worth of meth, arrests 5 Mexican suspects in major bust
item.description:
Nigeria seizes $220 million worth of meth, arrests 5 Mexican suspects in major bust
Nigeria’s anti-drug agency says it seized at least $220 million worth of methamphetamine and arrested five Mexican suspects in a major operation in the African country's southeastByDYEPKAZAH SHIBAYAN Associated PressNovember 25, 2026, 1:10 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
ABUJA, Nigeria -- ABUJA, Nigeria (AP) — Nigeria’s anti-drug agency on Wednesday announced the seizure of at least $220 million worth of methamphetamine and the arrest of five Mexican suspects in a major drug operation in the country's southeast.
The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency said its operatives stormed an industrial-scale laboratory in Enugu state where “Mexican meth specialists” were arrested. The Mexicans were allegedly recruited by a Nigerian national before entering the country with forged passports, agency spokesman Femi Babafemi said in a statement.
“A total of 1,512 kilograms of methamphetamine, finished and in production, with an estimated value of $226.8 million was recovered from the clandestine factory," Babafemi said.
It is one of the largest seizures this year in a country that has emerged as a hot spot for illegal drugs. A transnational drug syndicate involving Nigerians and Mexicans was busted in southwestern Nigeria in May, one of several such operations carried out recently.

item.title: Rescuers battle tough conditions in flooded Indonesian mine
item.description:
Rescuers battle tough conditions in flooded Indonesian mine
Rescuers are battling high water, darkness and slippery, narrow terrain while searching for miners believed trapped by flooding in an illegal gold mineByNINIEK KARMINI Associated PressNovember 25, 2026, 10:43 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
JAKARTA, Indonesia -- Rescuers battled high water, darkness and slippery, narrow terrain Thursday searching for 10 miners believed trapped by flooding in an illegal gold mine where 16 bodies have been recovered.
The miners were digging for grains of gold late Monday when heavy rain caused the Ciseureuh River to overflow into a mine shaft in the Bogor regency of West Java province. Several people escaped from one section of the excavation before floodwaters filled the shaft, estimated to be about 100 meters (330 feet) deep, in a mountainous area south of the capital, Jakarta.
Authorities said they were not immediately notified because the miners were operating illegally, and local miners and residents initially tried to pump water from the site themselves before the situation became unmanageable.
Police first received reports of trapped miners about 16 hours after the flooding occurred, and nearby state-owned mining company PT Antam forwarded a formal report to the Jakarta Search and Rescue Agency shortly after midnight Wednesday, triggering a full-scale rescue operation.
The search and rescue team used submersible water pumps to suck water from the hole and tried to close off openings where groundwater seeped in.
West Java police spokesperson Hendra Rochmawan said authorities believe at least 10 miners remain trapped as rescuers retrieved 16 bodies by Thursday.

item.title: Serbia sets presidential election for Dec. 27 after students won parliamentary vote
item.description:
Serbia sets presidential election for Dec. 27 after students won parliamentary vote
Serbia's Parliament speaker has set an early presidential election for December 27ByJOVANA GEC Associated PressNovember 26, 2026, 6:57 AM
BELGRADE, Serbia -- BELGRADE, Serbia (AP) — Serbia 's Parliament speaker on Thursday set an early presidential election for Dec. 27, after former President Aleksandar Vucic resigned in September to pursue what turned out to be a failed bid to become prime minister.
The presidential vote will be held after a student movement defeated Vucic's right-wing Serbian Progressive Party in an early parliamentary ballot on Oct. 25.
Vucic and his party had ruled virtually unchallenged for 14 years. He had run for prime minister after serving two near-complete five-year terms as president, and was banned by law from seeking a third term.
“I hope we will have a tough choice between top candidates and their programs," Speaker Aleksandar Cupic said. “Building democratic institutions is the task for all of us.”
It was not immediately clear who the presidential candidates will be. Vucic has suggested that his SNS party could sit out the election.

item.title: Spain's economy has grown under Sánchez, but many voters aren't feeling it. 5 charts explain why
item.description:
Spain's economy has grown under Sánchez, but many voters aren't feeling it. 5 charts explain why
Spain's economy is growing faster than most of Europe, but many Spaniards are struggling with high living costsBySUMAN NAISHADHAM Associated PressNovember 24, 2026, 10:49 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
MADRID -- Spain's economy has been growing faster than most of its European peers, but many Spaniards haven't felt the benefits. Discontent, particularly around soaring housing costs, is widespread and bound to be a decisive force in Sunday's national election.
On the campaign trail, incumbent Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has had to tread a careful line between boasting about Spain's enviable growth rates while acknowledging voters' frustration over the rising cost of living.
The progressive Spanish leader called an early election for Nov. 29 after weeks of nationwide protests over living conditions, hoping to capitalize on their anger. While Sánchez has warned voters that a right-wing government would not make their lives more affordable, his conservative opponents have slammed his government for doing too little.
These five charts illustrate the disconnect between Spain's economic growth under Sánchez and the financial pressures many voters face.
House prices in Spain rose 43% between 2015 and 2025 when adjusted for inflation, according to Eurostat’s house price index. Across the European Union, prices rose an average of 25% during the same period.
Market pressures and insufficient construction have driven prices even higher in Spain's largest cities and popular tourist destinations, putting homeownership beyond the reach of many young Spaniards.
Spain has a strong tradition of homeownership, but the Bank of Spain estimates the country of 50 million people has a shortage of 750,000 houses based on demand and the pace of new construction.

item.title: Amnesty calls for independent war crimes probe into Ethiopian shelling in Tigray
item.description:
Amnesty calls for independent war crimes probe into Ethiopian shelling in Tigray
Amnesty International called for a war crimes investigation into shelling by Ethiopian troops and an allied militia in Tigray, saying it verified 14 civilian deaths in four attacksByKHALED KAZZIHA Associated PressNovember 25, 2026, 5:35 AM
NAIROBI, Kenya -- Shelling of civilian neighborhoods in Tigray by Ethiopian forces and an allied militia should be investigated as possible war crimes, Amnesty International said Tuesday, as residents near the Eritrean border described military buildups and fears of another war.
Amnesty said it independently verified 14 civilian deaths in four artillery attacks on Alamata between Sept. 26-28, when Ethiopian forces and the allied Tigray Peace Forces advanced on the city.
It also accused forces allied with the Tigray People’s Liberation Front of endangering civilians by establishing military positions in residential areas and schools. The TPLF rejected those allegations in a written response to Amnesty.
The findings come amid renewed fighting in Tigray and growing fears of a wider confrontation between Ethiopia and neighboring Eritrea.
Amnesty interviewed residents, including survivors and medical personnel, and analyzed videos, photographs and satellite imagery.
The Ethiopian government and the military have so far not responded to the report by Amnesty. The human rights group said neither the military nor the allied militia had responded before publication.
Berhe Sibagadis, 41, a father of four in Alitena in Tigray’s Irob district, several kilometers from the border with Eritrea, is preparing to move his family further from the border region with neighboring Eritrea.
“I have to save my family, therefore I have to move to the center of Tigray,” he told The Associated Press by phone.
He said Eritrean forces are occupying a part of his local administration inside Ethiopia's borders.

item.title: US-backed Ebola quarantine center violated constitution, Kenyan court rules
item.description:
US-backed Ebola quarantine center violated constitution, Kenyan court rules
Kenya's government violated the constitution by allowing the construction of a U.S.-backed Ebola quarantine facility without public participation, the High Court has ruledByEVELYNE MUSAMBI Associated PressNovember 26, 2026, 7:16 AM
Share
NAIROBI, Kenya -- Kenya’s government violated the Constitution by allowing the construction of a U.S.-backed Ebola quarantine facility without public participation, a senior court ruled on Thursday.
The 50-bed facility at a military base in Laikipia sparked deadly protests by residents who feared exposure to the virus and an outbreak that could overwhelm Kenya's fragile health system.
In May, the High Court had ordered construction of the facility to be halted pending the determination of a case filed by the Law Society of Kenya and constitutional watchdog Katiba Institute. The petitioners argued that Kenya’s fragile health system was ill-equipped to handle a potential Ebola outbreak.
Trump administration officials had said Americans exposed to Ebola abroad would be sent to the facility rather than flown home. The U.S. government planned to commit $13.5 million to Kenya’s Ebola preparedness efforts.
Justice Patricia Nyaundi on Thursday ordered the government to disclose all agreements with the U.S. within 45 days. She also barred further construction or operations at the facility.

item.title: New Miss Universe's Puerto Rican hometown celebrates her historic win
item.description:
New Miss Universe's Puerto Rican hometown celebrates her historic win
The new Miss Universe hails from a Puerto Rican town whose people have long been known as “the cucumbers.”ByDÁNICA COTO Associated PressNovember 25, 2026, 9:33 AM
Share
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- The new Miss Universe hails from a Puerto Rican town whose residents have long been known as “the cucumbers.”
Nestled in the mountains of western Puerto Rico, San Sebastián has been celebrating since Jennifer Barreto made history late Tuesday as the first mother and first married woman to win Miss Universe.
“It was a day for the history books!” exclaimed one municipal worker at the mayor’s office, which was abuzz with excitement.
The town of some 39,000 people — named after its famous karst formations that look like cucumbers — could barely contain itself.
“La Barreto,” as she’s known, was on the lips of many across San Sebastián hours after the win.
“So excited!” said María Rivera as she juggled orders Wednesday morning at El Guayabal bakery. “We were sure she was going to win.”
Barreto, 27, has one daughter and holds master’s degrees in research psychology and clinical social work. She also works as a prevention specialist with the U.S. Department of Defense, developing strategies to combat harmful behaviors.
“Her journey is a powerful reminder that motherhood, marriage and personal ambition are not mutually exclusive, and that a woman’s potential should never be defined by the stage of life she is in,” Ronald Day, CEO of the Miss Universe Organization, said in a statement.
The organization began allowing married women and mothers to compete in 2023. The pageant has lost favor in some countries, with critics saying it objectifies women and promotes unrealistic body ideals.
Barreto is the sixth Puerto Rican woman to win the Miss Universe crown, ending a 20-year wait for the island.

item.title: Puerto Rico's Supreme Court cancels a key power contract and many wonder what's next
item.description:
Puerto Rico's Supreme Court cancels a key power contract and many wonder what's next
Puerto Rico’s Supreme Court has narrowly ruled in favor of canceling the government’s contract with Luma Energy, following a contentious legal fight with the private power companyByDÁNICA COTO Associated PressNovember 25, 2026, 12:48 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- Puerto Rico’s Supreme Court has narrowly ruled in favor of canceling the government’s contract with Luma Energy following a contentious legal fight with the private power company.
The 5-4 ruling of more than 200 pages, made public on Wednesday, plunges the island into further uncertainty as many wonder who will take over from Luma while power outages persist across the U.S. territory and crews continue to repair the grid razed by Hurricane Maria in 2017.
Puerto Rico’s government had sued Luma nearly a year ago, following up on a campaign promise made by Gov. Jenniffer González to cancel the contract.
The court awarded one year for officials to figure out their next steps. González said her administration would seek a new company and that transmission and distribution operations would not revert to Puerto Rico’s Electric Power Authority.
She blamed Luma for “constant interruptions" and “unnecessary outages,” asserting they have enough money to provide proper service as she accused them of lacking diligence and driving the cost of electricity in the U.S. territory to a record high.
“You have seen the substations on fire,” she said. “They have not yet been able to explain why.”
As the governor spoke, a federal control board that oversees the island's finances issued a statement saying its immediate concern is the continuity of service.
“The Puerto Rican government's decision to terminate the contract creates enormous uncertainty at a time when the people and businesses of Puerto Rico look for stability,” the board said, noting that there's no “clear plan or successor compan...
